title: Market or limit?
objectives: Choose an order type by trading price against certainty of execution.
Compare the expected costs of a market and a limit order with a fill-chance model.

screens.prose: You want 100 shares. You can buy now at the best ask, £100.14. Or you can bid £100.10, join the queue, and wait for a seller to come to you.
screens.question: Which is the honest comparison?

options.text: Waiting saves 4p a share if it fills, but it might never fill
Waiting saves 4p a share, so it is simply better
options.why: You counted the saving and ignored the risk. If the price rises before a seller arrives, you end up buying later at a worse price.

options.text: Both cost the same, because the mid is the same
options.why: The mid is the same, but the prices are not: £100.14 now, or £100.10 if a seller fills you.

hints.text: What happens to the waiting bid if buyers push the price up?
A bid at £100.10 fills only if a seller comes down to it.
Buying now is certain; waiting is cheaper only when it works.

feedback.correct: Price against certainty: that is the whole choice.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what happens if no seller ever comes down to £100.10.

explain.text: Buying now costs 4p more but is certain. Waiting is cheaper only if it fills, and if the price runs away you buy later for more. Every order choice trades price against certainty.

screens.prose: A simple model. Each tick (1p) below the ask cuts the chance of a fill by 0.1, so a bid at £100.10 fills with chance 0.6. If it misses, the price has ticked up and you buy at £100.15. Costs are measured from the mid, £100.12.

derive.caption: Limit £{{fixed(lim, 2)}}: fills with chance {{fixed(fp, 1)}}. Expected cost {{fixed(ec, 1)}}p a share against the mid.

screens.question: Slide the limit price down from £100.14. Where is the expected cost lowest?

options.text: At £100.14, buying at the ask
options.why: At the ask you fill for sure but pay 2p a share. Moving down lowers the expected cost for a while.

options.text: At £100.09 or £100.10, around the best bid
At £100.04, as low as the slider goes
options.why: You took a lower limit as cheaper. At £100.04 it never fills, so you always chase and pay 3p.

hints.text: Watch the expected cost in the caption at each stop of the slider.

feedback.correct: The cost bottoms out near the best bid.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the expected cost in the caption at each price.

explain.text: The expected cost falls from 2.0p at the ask to 0.0p at £100.10 or £100.09, then rises again: 1.2p at £100.06 and 3.0p at £100.04. A limit far from the market rarely fills, so it is not free.

screens.prose: A **market order** buys now at the ask. A **limit order** names a price and waits. Use the model to fill in the expected cost of each, in pence a share against the mid. The limit sits at the bid.
screens.question: Fill in the missing costs.

hints.text: A market order always fills, so its expected cost is its cost.
If the limit misses, you buy at £100.15. How far is that above the mid?
Expected cost of the limit: $0.6 \times (-2) + 0.4 \times 3$.

feedback.correct: Market 2p, limit 0p: the limit wins here, on average.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each cost by its chance.

byKey.r1c3: If the bid misses, the price has ticked up to £100.15. That is 3p above the £100.12 mid.
byKey.r1c4: Weight each cost by its chance: $0.6 \times (-2) + 0.4 \times 3$.
byKey.r0c4: A market order fills for sure at £100.14, 2p above the mid.

explain.text: The market order costs the half-spread, 2p, every time. The limit earns 2p with chance 0.6 and pays 3p with chance 0.4: $-1.2 + 1.2 = 0$. On average waiting saves 2p a share here.

screens.prose: Same share, but a much longer queue sits at £100.10. Now the bid fills with chance only 0.3. A miss still costs 3p.
screens.question: What is the expected cost of the limit order, in pence a share?

hints.text: Weight the two costs by their new chances.
Fill: chance 0.3, cost −2p. Miss: chance 0.7, cost 3p.

feedback.correct: 1.5p: still below the market order's 2p, but only just.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each cost by its chance, then add.

byKey.old: That is the answer for a fill chance of 0.6. The longer queue lowers it to 0.3.
byKey.fill-only: You counted only the fill. With chance 0.7 the bid misses and costs 3p.
byKey.miss-only: You counted only the miss. With chance 0.3 the bid fills and earns 2p.

explain.text: $0.3 \times (-2) + 0.7 \times 3 = 1.5$p. A lower fill chance moves the limit's cost towards the miss cost. The saving over the market order has shrunk from 2p to 0.5p.

screens.prose: Between a fill chance of 0.3 and 0 there is a point where the two orders cost the same.
screens.question: At what fill chance does the limit cost exactly as much as the market order?

hints.text: Set the limit's expected cost equal to 2p.

feedback.correct: At a fill chance of 0.2 the two orders cost the same.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $-2p + 3(1 - p) = 2$ for $p$.

byKey.half: A coin flip is a guess, not the break-even. Solve $-2p + 3(1 - p) = 2$.
byKey.bid-chance: 0.6 is the fill chance at the bid in the first model. Solve for the chance that makes the costs equal.
byKey.third: You dropped the $-2p$ term: $3 - 3p = 2$ gives $\tfrac{1}{3}$. Keep both terms: $3 - 5p = 2$.

explain.text: $-2p + 3 - 3p = 2$, so $p = 0.2$. Above a fill chance of 0.2 the limit is cheaper on average; below it the market order wins.

screens.prose: News is due and the price is jumping. A bid at £100.10 fills with chance 0.5. If it misses, the price has run 6 ticks and you buy at £100.20, 8p above the mid.
screens.question: Which order has the lower expected cost?

options.text: The market order: 2p against 3p
The limit order, because limits are cheaper
options.why: You took 'limit orders are cheaper' as a rule. Here a miss costs 8p: $0.5 \times (-2) + 0.5 \times 8 = 3$p, more than the market order's 2p.

options.text: They cost the same
options.why: Work out the limit: $0.5 \times (-2) + 0.5 \times 8 = 3$p, against 2p for the market order.

hints.text: Work out the limit's expected cost with the new miss cost.
Fill: chance 0.5, cost −2p. Miss: chance 0.5, cost 8p.
$0.5 \times (-2) + 0.5 \times 8 = 3$p. Compare with 2p.

feedback.correct: When a miss is expensive, certainty is worth paying for.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the limit's expected cost before choosing.

byKey.limit: You took 'limit orders are cheaper' as a rule. Here a miss costs 8p: $0.5 \times (-2) + 0.5 \times 8 = 3$p, more than the market order's 2p.

explain.text: The limit costs 3p on average, the market order 2p. It is worse still: a bid tends to fill just as the price falls through it, so a fill is often a bad buy. That is **adverse selection**, the subject of level 3.

screens.prose: A thinly traded share has best bid £4.90 and best ask £5.10. A market buy pays 10p a share over the £5.00 mid, 2% of the price. You are a patient buyer.
screens.question: Where is the natural place for your limit buy?

options.text: At the mid, £5.00: you give up half the gap and stand first at a new best bid
At the bid, £4.90
options.why: You copied the best bid. Behind 2,000 shares you may wait all day, and the wide gap leaves room to step in front.

options.text: Nowhere: send a market order
options.why: You pay 10p a share, 2% of the price, for speed a patient buyer does not need.

hints.text: A 20p gap leaves room for a bid between the two sides.
Any bid above £4.90 goes to the front of a new line.
Halfway, £5.00, costs nothing against the mid and is first in line.

feedback.correct: In a wide spread, the mid is the natural limit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the room inside the gap.

explain.text: In a very wide spread a mid-point limit is the natural choice. It costs nothing against the mid and jumps the whole queue at £4.90. Some venues offer mid-point orders that do this for you.

screens.prose: Write $h$ for the half-spread, $p$ for the fill chance and $h + c$ for the cost of a miss. Against the mid: $$E[\text{market}] = h, \qquad E[\text{limit}] = -p\,h + (1 - p)(h + c)$$ In our model $h = 2$p and $c = 1$p.
screens.question: Which change makes the limit order more attractive?

options.text: A higher fill chance $p$
A higher miss cost $c$
options.why: A bigger $c$ makes each miss dearer, so the limit looks worse, as in the news trap.

options.text: A smaller half-spread $h$
options.why: A smaller $h$ shrinks what the limit saves when it fills, and what the market order pays.

hints.text: Which term is a saving, and which is a cost?
The $-p\,h$ term is the saving. It grows with $p$.

feedback.correct: More fills mean more saving and fewer chases.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at which terms grow or shrink.

explain.text: Raising $p$ moves weight from the miss, $h + c$, to the saving, $-h$. Raising $c$ makes misses dearer. Urgency, size and volatility all raise $c$.

screens.prose: When is the limit cheaper? We want $E[\text{limit}] < E[\text{market}]$ and solve for $p$. Your break-even of 0.2 should drop out.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $-p\,h + (1 - p)(h + c) < h$, the limit must cost less
$-p\,h + h + c - p\,h - p\,c < h$, expand the bracket
$c < p\,(2h + c)$, take $h$ from both sides and move the $p$ terms right
$p > \dfrac{c}{2h + c}$, divide by $2h + c$, which is positive

hints.text: Start from the inequality that says the limit is cheaper.
Expand $(1 - p)(h + c)$ before collecting the $p$ terms.
After expanding, the $h$ on each side cancels, leaving $c - 2p\,h - p\,c < 0$.

feedback.correct: $p > c/(2h + c)$: with $h = 2$ and $c = 1$ that is $1/5 = 0.2$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from the comparison, expand, collect, then divide.

byKey.s3: The $p$ terms can only be collected once the bracket is expanded.
byKey.s4: Dividing by $2h + c$ is the last step, once $p$ multiplies a single bracket.

explain.text: With $h = 2$ and $c = 1$, $p > 1/(4 + 1) = 0.2$, the break-even you found. A big miss cost pushes the threshold towards 1: almost no fill chance is good enough.

screens.prose: An index fund must own its new weights at today's closing price, set in the 4.30 pm closing auction. A market maker in the same share posts bids and asks all day.
screens.question: Which pairing fits each one's needs?

options.text: Fund: orders in the closing auction, or market orders. Market maker: passive limit quotes.
Fund: limit orders at the bid all day, to save the spread
options.why: You applied the market maker's tactic to the fund. Shares unfilled at 4.30 pm leave it off its benchmark, so its miss cost is huge.

options.text: Market maker: market orders, to be sure of trading
options.why: A market maker earns the spread by being filled at its own prices. Crossing the spread pays it away.

hints.text: For each, what does a missed fill cost?
The fund is judged against the closing price. The market maker is paid to wait.
Large $c$ favours certainty; small $c$ and a job of earning $h$ favour waiting.

feedback.correct: Certainty for the fund, patience for the market maker.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare what a miss costs each of them.

explain.text: The fund's miss cost $c$ is large, so $c/(2h + c)$ is near 1 and certainty wins: it trades in the auction at the closing price. The market maker's $c$ is small and its job is to earn $h$, so it posts limits and waits.

ideas: A market order is certain and pays the half-spread; a limit order may earn it but may not fill.
Expected cost weights the saving by the fill chance and the chase by the miss chance.
The limit wins when $p > c/(2h + c)$; urgency, size and volatility raise $c$ and favour the market order.

formula.name: Market or limit
formula.note: Choose the limit when $p > c/(2h + c)$.

summary.trap: A limit order is not always cheaper. A miss costs money, and a far-away limit almost always misses.

quiz.prose: Half-spread 2p. A limit at the bid fills with chance 0.8 and saves 2p; a miss costs 3p.
quiz.question: What is the limit's expected cost, in pence a share against the mid?

feedback.correct: −1p: on average the limit earns a penny a share.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each cost by its chance.

byKey.fill-only: You counted only the fill. With chance 0.2 it misses and costs 3p.
byKey.sign: A filled bid earns 2p, so its cost is −2p. Keep the sign.

explain.text: $0.8 \times (-2) + 0.2 \times 3 = -1.6 + 0.6 = -1$p. A negative cost means the order earns, on average, against the mid.

quiz.prose: A trader posts a buy limit 50p below the market. He says: "If it never fills, it cost me nothing." He still needs the shares by the end of the day.
quiz.question: What is wrong with his claim?

options.text: A miss has a cost: he must buy later, often at a higher price
The exchange charges a fee for unfilled orders
options.why: Resting orders are usually free to post. The cost comes from having to buy later anyway.

options.text: Nothing: an unfilled order costs nothing
options.why: You took 'no trade' as 'no cost'. He still needs the shares, and the price may have risen by then.

feedback.correct: Not trading is a cost when you need to trade.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what he does at the end of the day if it never fills.

explain.text: Far from the market the fill chance is near 0, so the expected cost is nearly the full miss cost. A limit is only cheap if it has a real chance of filling.

quiz.prose: A share's spread is 10p, so $h = 5$p. A miss costs $h + c$ with $c = 2$p.
quiz.question: Above what fill chance is the limit cheaper than the market order?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $p > c/(2h + c)$.

byKey.h-c: You used $c/(h + c) = 2/7$. The bottom is $2h + c$: the saving and the half-spread on a miss both count.
byKey.over-h: You used $c/h = 2/5$. The bottom is $2h + c = 12$.

explain.text: $p > \dfrac{c}{2h + c} = \dfrac{2}{10 + 2} = \dfrac{1}{6}$. A wider spread lowers the bar, because each fill saves more.

quiz.prose: A trader must buy 2,000 shares now to hedge an options position that loses £500 for every 1p the share rises.
quiz.question: Which order fits?

options.text: A market order: the miss cost is far bigger than the spread
A limit at the bid, to save the spread
options.why: You chased the spread saving. Each penny of delay risks £500, so the miss cost dwarfs 2p a share.

options.text: A limit well below the bid, in case the price dips
options.why: That rarely fills. While it waits, the hedge stays open.

feedback.correct: Urgency means a large $c$, and a large $c$ means certainty.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare what waiting risks with what it saves.

explain.text: The half-spread on 2,000 shares is 2p a share, £40 in all. A single penny against the open hedge costs £500. With a miss cost that large, the break-even fill chance is near 1, so the market order wins.
